finding: §10.3 says "Every round MUST record to `rounds/<n>/summary.json`" counts for raised, deduplicated, suppressed by thread, waived, forced to question, drafted, posted, and both discard dispositions — but no command anywhere in the spec is given the job of writing that file, and two of those counts are only knowable at a stage that has no per-PR state to write to. §6.4.4 and §9.3.6 both drop records at merge and say the count "reaches the round summary"; §9.3.6 is explicit that the drop happens "at merge" and that dropped findings "MUST NOT be written to `findings.ndjson` at all". So by the time `cr record` runs, the waived and already-posted findings are gone from its input and it cannot count them. §2.3 gives `cr merge` no output file, and §11 describes it as a file-to-file command with `-o <out>`. §10.1.6 and §11.1 then require `cr status` to always print those counts from durable state that nothing wrote.
suggestion: Name the writer of `rounds/<n>/summary.json` and the accumulation order — e.g. `cr merge` writes its drop counts into the current round's summary (it already takes `--repo` and `--pr` for exactly this class of reason), `cr draft` and `cr post --confirm` update their fields, and `cr status` only reads. If merge must stay stateless, move the §6.4.4/§9.3.6 drops to `cr record` and say so in both places.

finding: §3.4.1 puts a unit's line numbers in two coordinate spaces — RIGHT for a hunk that adds lines, LEFT for a hunk that adds none — and then §3.4.4, §3.4.5, and §3.4.6 all do arithmetic across them without saying whether hunks of different sides may share a unit. §3.4.4 clusters when "the gap between the last changed line of one and the first changed line of the next is at most `cluster.gap_lines`": for a RIGHT-numbered hunk followed by a LEFT-numbered deletion hunk in the same file this subtracts numbers from different files, and the gap can be negative when the PR deleted lines earlier in the file. §3.4.5 splits "in ascending start order" over the same mixed keys, and §3.4.6 orders the unit-hash pre-image by "ascending line order" within a file over the same mixed keys. Three competent engineers produce three different unit sets: partition by side before clustering; compare raw integers; or translate LEFT positions into RIGHT positions via the hunk header. Because the unit hash is derived from that ordering and §10.2.2 gates completeness on the unit hash, the disagreement propagates from clustering to whether a round can ever be reported complete.
suggestion: State in §3.4.4 that clustering partitions a file's hunks by the side their line numbers are on per §3.4.1 and that adjacency, the §3.4.5 split order, and the §3.4.6 hash ordering are all evaluated within one side only, so a unit never mixes sides — or, if mixing is intended, define the single coordinate space all three rules use and how a LEFT position maps into it.

finding: §4.5.5 enumerates the coverage cell's fields — unit id, role id, one of `pass`/`finding`/`question`/`na`, head, unit hash, and a reason when `na` — but three other sections require a cell to carry data that has no field there. §4.1.5: when a note explains an unmapped unit "the coverage cell MUST cite the note id". §4.4.1: the covered / partially covered / uncovered classification "MUST be recorded in the coverage cell together with the test paths it rested on". §3.6.6: "any coverage cell or record citing a retracted note MUST be reported as needing re-evaluation", which presupposes a stored note reference. §4.5.6 then makes `cr cells record` reject malformed cells with exit code 1 — against a schema that is incomplete, so I cannot write the validator or the struct.
suggestion: Extend §4.5.5 with the missing optional fields and their conditions: `note_id` (required when a cell is `pass` because a note explained an unmapped unit, per §4.1.5), `test_coverage` (`covered`, `partial`, `uncovered`; required for cells on the test axis) and `test_paths` (required with it, per §4.4.1). State which are agent-supplied and which `cr` computes, so §4.5.6's rejection and §6.1.4's computed-field rule both have something to check.

finding: §5.1.2 and §5.1.3 and §5.1.6 contradict each other for tracked files, and the contradiction is an unbounded loop rather than a one-off failure. §5.1.6 defines **clean** as "no tracked file differs from HEAD", and carves out only untracked files as expected output of `sandbox.copy` and `sandbox.setup`. But `sandbox.copy` copies arbitrary "paths from the main worktree", which include tracked files the developer has modified locally, and `sandbox.setup` runs arbitrary commands — `composer install` and `npm install` routinely rewrite tracked lock files, and build steps touch tracked generated files. Any such profile makes the sandbox permanently unclean: every probe triggers "MUST be recreated", recreation re-runs copy and setup, the next check fails again, and no probe or test run ever executes. The failure is silent in the sense that §5.1.6's recreation is the documented, mandatory response.
suggestion: Take the post-create state as the baseline rather than HEAD. After `sandbox.copy` and `sandbox.setup` complete, record the sandbox's tracked-file state (for example a `git status --porcelain` snapshot or per-path hashes) in per-PR state, and define **clean** in §5.1.6 as "no tracked file differs from that recorded post-setup state, and no leftover probe artefact exists". That still catches an unreverted mutation, which is what §5.1.6 exists for, without treating deliberate setup output as corruption.

finding: A gap probe can essentially never reach a `probed` grade, because its baseline cannot pass. §5.4.4 requires the probe to support a finding "only when its baseline passed per §5.2.5". §5.5 defines `baseline` as the run record "at the same head whose filter equals this probe's", and §5.2.2 says the filtered baseline runs "on unmutated code" — i.e. before the supplied test file is placed. §5.4.3 rung 3 makes clear the filter is expected to select the supplied test ("the executed test count is known and equals zero, so the filter excluded the supplied test"). Compose those: the baseline runs that same filter with the probe file absent, selects zero tests, and §5.2.5 says a run with `tests_run` not greater than zero has `passed: false` and "cannot serve as a baseline". So the natural filter makes §5.4.4's precondition permanently false, and every gap probe is capped at `argued` and posted as a question. The spec never says how a gap probe's baseline is to be constructed differently from a mutation probe's.
suggestion: Define the gap probe's baseline separately from the mutation probe's: it MUST be an unfiltered (or profile-default) baseline run at the same head, so it measures whether the pre-existing suite is green rather than whether the not-yet-placed test exists. Alternatively define the filtered gap baseline as running with the probe file placed but before the assertion, and say so. Also state which command creates a baseline when none exists, and what `cr probe run` does when it cannot find one — `baseline` is a required field in §5.5 with no defined producer at probe time.

finding: A gap probe can never reach `probed` under the natural filter. §5.5 defines `baseline` (required for both kinds) as "the run record at the same head whose filter equals this probe's", and §5.2.2 requires that filtered baseline to be run "on unmutated code". For a gap probe the supplied test file does not exist on unmutated code, so a filter narrow enough to select it — which §5.4.3 rung 3 assumes, since a filter that excludes it yields `no-tests-selected` — selects zero tests in the baseline. Round 6's repair to §5.2.5 now makes `passed` require `tests_run > 0`, so that baseline is `passed: false`, and §5.4.4's "only when its baseline passed per §5.2.5" is unsatisfiable. The gap probe's only path to `probed`, and to severity `high`, is dead. The `baseline` concept was defined for mutation probes, where the same tests exist before and after, and does not transfer.
suggestion: Define `baseline` per kind in §5.5. For `mutation`, keep the current definition. For `gap`, the baseline is the run at the same head with the same filter **with the probe file absent**, and its role is only to establish that the pre-existing suite under that filter was not already failing — so state that a gap-probe baseline selecting zero tests is admissible and does not block support, or require the gap-probe baseline to be the unfiltered run of §5.2.2. Whichever is chosen, §5.4.4 must name it.

finding: `baseline` is a required probe field defined only as "Id of the run record (§5.2.4) at the same head whose filter equals this probe's", and nothing says how `cr probe run` obtains it in the two cases that actually occur. (a) No such run record exists — a probe run before any `cr test` at this head. Does `cr probe run` execute the baseline itself, or refuse, and with which exit code? §5.2.2's "A baseline run with no filter MUST be recorded once per head" and "A filtered probe MUST additionally record a filtered baseline" state that one must exist without naming the command that creates it or the failure when it does not. (b) More than one matches — `cr test --filter x` run twice at the same head appends two records per §5.2.4, and nothing tie-breaks first vs. last. Case (b) is grade-flipping: §5.3.5 grants `probed` only when the baseline has `passed: true`, so choosing the earlier passing run over the later failing one manufactures exactly the evidence §5.3.5 exists to prevent. I would write "probe with no prior baseline exits 4"; another engineer writes "probe auto-records the baseline and succeeds"; both are faithful to the text.
suggestion: Add a rule to §5.2 naming the resolution: `cr probe run` MUST record the matching baseline itself when none exists at the current head for the probe's filter (counting it as a run, not a probe, against §5.6.4), and MUST select the most recent run record at the current head whose filter equals the probe's when several exist. State the exit code for the case where recording the baseline itself fails.

finding: "inside/outside the record's own unit" is the grading predicate in two places and is never defined. The §6.2 table grants `cited` when a citation "lies outside the record's own unit", and §6.2.2 grants `probed` only when a probe's `target` "falls inside that record's unit". §3.4.6 says a unit records "its file paths, its hunk ranges", but a hunk range may mean the full diff-hunk header span (context lines included) or only the changed-line extent, and nothing says whether membership requires the path to be one of the unit's files. The two readings push the two grades in opposite directions: the narrow reading makes more citations `cited` (may assert), the wide reading makes more probes supporting (may assert). Worse, §5.5's `target` is "validated as §6.2.3 validates a citation", i.e. against the current head (RIGHT side), while a deletion-only unit's hunk ranges are LEFT-side line numbers per §3.4.1 — so for such a unit the predicate is either always false or compares two coordinate spaces. I cannot write the grading tests without picking one of at least four incompatible definitions, and each pick changes which records may assert.
suggestion: Add a numbered rule under §6.2 defining containment once: a `path:line` is inside unit `u` when `path` is one of `u`'s file paths and `line` falls within one of `u`'s recorded hunk ranges on the same side as that hunk's line numbering per §3.4.1, where a hunk range is the closed interval from its first to its last changed line (context lines excluded). State that a probe `target` is compared on the same side as the unit's hunk, and that a target on the other side never falls inside. Then have the §6.2 `cited` row and §6.2.2 both reference that rule by number.

finding: §6.2.2 binds a probe to a record by unit containment — "A probe supports a record only when its `target` falls inside that record's unit, so one experiment cannot grade an unrelated finding" — but the `so` clause claims more than the rule delivers. §5.5.2 caps the finding-to-probe direction ("A finding MUST reference at most one probe") and nothing caps the probe-to-finding direction, so a single probe may be referenced by every record in its unit. A unit is up to `cluster.max_lines` changed lines wide (default 80, §3.4.4-5), spans multiple hunks, and may span multiple files (§3.4.6 records "its file paths", plural). Worse, §3.4.5 makes an oversized single hunk one unit where "the limit does not bind" — an unbounded unit. So one mutation at line 10 that no test caught grades a finding about line 78, or about a different file in the same unit, or anywhere inside an arbitrarily large oversized unit, as `probed`: the assertion register, the maximum severity of §5.4.4, and (per the finding above) no visible evidence. That is exactly the unrelated-finding grading §6.2.2's rationale says it prevents. One experiment is being spent to buy the assertion register for N unproven claims, which is the cheapest possible way to convert credibility into recall.
suggestion: Bind the probe to the record's anchor, not to its unit: require the probe's `target` to fall within the record's `anchor.start_line`..`anchor.line` range on the same path, or within a small fixed proximity of it, and state the rationale in terms the rule actually delivers. If unit-level binding must be kept for practicality, then at minimum forbid an oversized unit (§3.4.5) from carrying probe-based grading at all, and cap the number of records one probe may grade at one.

finding: The merge-to-record pipeline is self-blocking. §6.5.1 requires `cr merge` to "apply §6.4", and §6.4.3 stamps `state: duplicate` and `duplicate_of` on suppressed duplicates; §6.5.1 also requires merge to report counts by grade, which it can only do by computing `grade`. But merge's output file is `cr record`'s input file, and §6.1.4 requires `cr record` to reject with exit code 1 any record arriving with `grade`, `state`, or `duplicate_of`. §9.1's closing note pulls the other way, asserting "`cr merge` is not a producer" and that "§6.4.3 marks duplicates as `cr record` writes them". As written, either merge emits the computed fields and every record is rejected, or merge does not apply §6.4.3 and §6.5.1 is wrong. Nothing distinguishes the merge output schema from the record input schema.
suggestion: Split §6.4 explicitly by executor: state that `cr merge` applies §6.4.1, §6.4.2, §6.4.4, and §9.3.6 — grouping, representative selection, and line-level drops, all of which remove or order lines rather than stamping fields — and that `cr record` alone writes `state`, `grade`, and `duplicate_of` per §6.4.3, re-deriving the grouping from §6.4.1's key. Add a sentence to §6.5.1 saying merge computes grades internally for its counts and MUST NOT write `grade` into the output file, so §6.1.4 stays absolute.

finding: `cr merge`'s output file is the input to `cr record`, and the two contracts collide. §6.5.1 says merge MUST "apply §6.4" and report counts by grade; §6.4.2 orders duplicates by grade and §6.4.3 requires suppressed duplicates to be "retained in state `duplicate` with `duplicate_of` naming the representative". But §6.1.4 says the agent MUST NOT write `grade`, `state`, or `duplicate_of` and "a record arriving with one MUST be rejected with exit code 1", and §6.1.3 names `cr merge` and `cr record` as the two commands that validate arriving records. So if merge stamps what §6.4 tells it to stamp, `cr record` must reject every line of merged.ndjson. §9.1's closing note pulls the other way: "`cr merge` is not a producer... §6.4.3 marks duplicates as `cr record` writes them." I cannot tell whether merge computes grades and duplicate_of and record trusts them, or merge only reports and record re-runs the whole of §6.4.
suggestion: State explicitly which stage owns which part of §6.4. Suggested split: merge computes grade and dedup in memory for its report and for the §6.4.4/§9.3.6 drops, but emits records carrying no computed field; `cr record` recomputes grade, re-runs §6.4.1–3, and is the sole writer of `grade`, `state`, and `duplicate_of`. Then say in §6.1.4 that the rejection applies to any input file, merged or per-role, so merge output is not a special case.

finding: §7.1.5 and §8.1.3 specify two different pre-images for the same hash. §7.1.5: "`cr` MUST write every body exactly as rendered to `rounds/<n>/rendered.json`, together with the normalised hash of the whole draft file. This is the only observable basis for detecting a user edit." §8.1.3: "§8.1.5, §7.1.5, and §7.1.6 apply to the agent region alone." One says whole file, the other says agent region only, and the draft file demonstrably contains `cr`-owned regions — §8.1.7 says the citation block "MUST NOT be editable through the draft", which presupposes it is in the draft. The two readings also behave differently: a whole-file hash changes whenever `cr` regenerates a citation block per §8.1.7, so regeneration alone registers as a user edit, while an agent-region hash does not. This is a single stored value with two mandated definitions, and §7.1.6's preservation rule ("preserve bodies for records whose body differs from `rendered.json`") reads off it, so the contradiction decides whether an edited body survives regeneration.
suggestion: Rewrite §7.1.5 to name one pre-image explicitly: store per record the agent region exactly as rendered, plus a normalised hash computed over the concatenation of the agent regions in draft order, and drop "the whole draft file". Then delete §7.1.5 from §8.1.3's scoping list, since the scope now lives in §7.1.5 itself.

finding: Every no-resurrection guarantee in the spec is keyed on `class`, and `class` is unconstrained agent-composed text. §7.4.1 keys a waiver by `(anchor.path, class, normalised hash of the anchored lines)`; §9.3.6 keys the posted index "exactly as a §7.4.1 waiver is"; §6.4.1 dedups by `(anchor.path, anchor.line, class)`. §6.1's schema defines `class` only as "Kebab-case defect class" — there is no enumeration, no registry, no canonicalisation, no per-PR stability requirement, and nothing that makes two independent role contexts, or the same role in a later round, choose the same slug for the same defect. §7.4.1 excludes `summary` from the key with an explicit rationale — "it is agent-composed prose that differs between rounds, and including it would let a waived finding resurface under a reworded summary" — and that rationale applies verbatim to `class`, which was kept. Two consequences reach the colleague. A finding the reviewer explicitly marked `disposition=wrong` returns next round under `n-plus-one-query` where the waiver holds `n-plus-one`, defeating VISION §2.5 and re-posting a known false positive. And §6.4.1 fails to collapse the same defect raised by two roles when their slugs differ, so the author receives duplicate comments on one line — the §1.6 volume cost, paid on the class of finding cr is least sure of. Rule-produced records are safe because §2.6's `class` is fixed per rule file; every agent-produced record is not.
suggestion: Make `class` an identity, not prose. Either (a) require every record's `class` to name an entry in a per-repository class registry under `~/.cr/repos/<owner>/<repo>/classes.json`, seeded by `cr init` and extended explicitly, rejecting an unknown class with exit code 1; or (b) at minimum require cr to canonicalise `class` at record time (lowercase, collapse separators, strip a trailing noun) and to key waivers, the posted index, and dedup on the canonical form, and state in §6.1 that the agent MUST reuse an existing class from the PR's corpus where one fits. §4.6.2 should carry the PR's existing class vocabulary into every role prompt so independent roles converge.

finding: The render contract carries citations to the reader but never the probe. §6.2.6 requires every citation of a `cited` record to be rendered verbatim "so the human makes the judgement `cr` cannot", and §8.1.7 mandates a `cr`-owned citation block. There is no equivalent for `probed`, which is the only grade that licenses an assertion. §8.1.3 fixes a posted comment at three regions — label, agent body, citation block — none of which carries the probe id, the mutation or test input, the result, or the output tail; §7.1.1's draft marker carries `grade` but not `probe`, so the probe does not reach the draft either. §5.4.4's "the probe output offered as a reproduction" names no channel. The result is that cr's strongest claim is the one posted with the least visible support, inverting the evidence ladder the whole design rests on.
suggestion: Add a §8.1.8 requiring a `cr`-owned probe block beneath the body of every `probed` record, generated by template substitution from the stored probe record and naming the probe id, kind, result, filter, and target, with the reproduction command. Give it the same treatment as §8.1.7: regenerated at render and post time, not editable through the draft, edits discarded. Extend §7.1.1's marker to carry `probe` so the block is regenerable from the draft alone.

finding: §8.1.3 introduces `<!-- cr:begin -->` / `<!-- cr:end -->` as the boundary between agent-written and `cr`-owned text, but leaves the parse undefined and the delimiters unprotected. Two problems make read-back untestable. First, the same undifferentiated pair delimits both `cr`-owned regions (the §8.1.4 label and the §8.1.7 citation block) with no region identifier, so recovery depends on an unstated positional convention — first pair is the label, last pair is the citations — which breaks for a record that has only one of them. Second, §8.1.3 forbids only "the marker comment" inside a body; nothing forbids an agent body containing `<!-- cr:begin -->` or `<!-- cr:end -->`. A body carrying either one re-partitions the comment, and since `cr` "regenerates their contents and discards any edit inside them", the discard can silently delete reader-facing prose from a posted comment, or displace the label whose protection §2.7 raises to the level of the confirmation gate. There is no specified behaviour to assert: reject, escape, first-match split, and last-match split are all consistent with the text and produce different posted bytes.
suggestion: Give each region its own delimiter (`<!-- cr:label -->`…`<!-- cr:/label -->`, `<!-- cr:citations -->`…`<!-- cr:/citations -->`) so recovery does not depend on position, and extend §8.1.3's prohibition: a body containing any `cr:`-prefixed HTML comment MUST abort with exit code 1 naming the record id, exactly as the marker comment does. State that an unbalanced or missing delimiter aborts rather than being repaired.

finding: §8.1.6 requires weak provenance to be disclosed "in the posted body, not only in the draft the author never sees" — a machine-generated suggestion must be labelled, and a record resting on a `source: note` claim must name the note and its source. §8.1.3 now makes the comment "exactly three regions in order: the §8.1.4 label, the agent body, and the §8.1.7 citation block", with the first and third cr-owned and regenerated. Neither cr-owned region carries provenance, so §8.1.6's disclosure can only live in the agent body — the one region cr regenerates nothing in, validates nothing about, and per §8.1.2 hands entirely to the agent. There is no check analogous to §8.1.5's `?` test, so a body that omits the disclosure posts silently. The spec proves it knows the pattern: §8.1.4 gets its own cr-owned line precisely because "§6.3's forcing reaches the reader through this line alone", and §8.1.7 gets one because "cr cannot judge whether a citation supports the summary". The identical argument was not applied to §8.1.6, and it applies with more force: a `source: note` claim rests on what §3.6.6 calls "unverified hearsay", and a `suggestion_origin: rule` suggestion is a regex substitution §2.6.2.4 admits cr cannot show compiles. Both post as one-click-actionable assertions with the disclosure that would let the author discount them optional in practice.
suggestion: Give §8.1.6 a cr-owned region. Extend §8.1.3's enumeration to four regions by folding provenance into the §8.1.4 label region (or adding a cr-owned provenance line beneath it), generated by template substitution from `suggestion_origin` and the `claim`'s `source`/`note_id`, regenerated at render and post time and non-editable through the draft. Failing that, add a §8.1.5-style validation: cr MUST refuse to post a record whose claim has `source: note`, or whose suggestion has `suggestion_origin: rule`, when the agent body does not contain the required disclosure token, with exit code 1 naming the record id.

finding: The strongest register posts with no cr-owned evidence, while the weaker one does. §8.1.7 gives every `cited` record a cr-owned, non-editable citation block listing each `path:line`, on the reasoning that the human must be able to check what cr cannot. No such region exists for a `probed` record. §8.1.3 declares a posted comment to be "exactly three regions in order: the §8.1.4 label, the agent body, and the §8.1.7 citation block", so a `probed` finding reaches the author as agent prose alone — the probe id, kind, target, result, filter, and baseline never leave `probes.ndjson`. The grade is computed honestly by §6.2.1, but what a mutation probe actually establishes is narrow ("no test failed when this target line was mutated, against a passing baseline"), and nothing constrains the agent's Turkish body from widening it into "this branch is untested" or "this is a data-loss bug" in the assertion register. §6.2.4 bars cr from ever calling a `cited` record verified or proven; there is no parallel restraint on how a `probed` record may be characterised, and no material for the reader to check it against. The gap reaches the human triager too: §7.1.1's marker field list (`id`, `kind`, `path`, `start_line`, `line`, `severity`, `grade`, `disposition`) has no `probe`, so the person doing the read-before-send cannot see which experiment backs the one register that asserts. VISION §1.3 makes converting a claim into a proof the differentiator; posting the proof-free prose of a proof spends the credibility the experiment bought without transferring the experiment.
suggestion: Extend §8.1.7's cr-owned region to `probed` records: append a cr-owned, regenerated, non-editable evidence block carrying the probe kind, `target`, `result`, `filter`, and the `baseline` run's verdict, phrased as the literal observation ("mutation at path:line; N tests ran, 0 failed; baseline passed") and nothing more. Add a §6.2.4-style restraint forbidding cr from describing a probe as proving anything wider than its recorded result. Add `probe` to §7.1.1's marker field list so the human triager sees the backing experiment at triage time.

finding: §10.2 repaired one certainty overstatement and left three of the same shape. Its closing paragraph requires the complete verdict to be printed together with the disabled and unavailable axes, "because completeness across three axes is not completeness across four". Three other mechanisms bound how much a round could establish, and none travels with the verdict. `probe.max_per_round` (§5.6.4, default 10) truncates evidence gathering, which not only leaves findings ungraded but leaves findings undisproved — §5.3.6 makes a `failed` mutation probe the thing that stops a finding being raised at all, so a bound cap systematically converts "would have been disproved" into "posted as a question". `test.max_edge_cases` (§4.4.2, default 10) truncates the enumeration that §4.4 rests on. And an `oversized` unit (§3.4.5) is a unit of unbounded size that fills exactly one cell per role, so a full matrix over it proves close to nothing while §10.2.2 counts it as a complete row. All three are reported somewhere — §10.1.1, §11.1, §4.4.2, §10.3 — but the verdict is the sentence a reader takes away, and it currently asserts completeness across a review whose depth was capped without saying so. P6 says coverage is proven; a cell over an unbounded unit is a claim, not a proof.
suggestion: Extend §10.2's closing paragraph so the complete verdict MUST be printed together with the disabled and unavailable axes, the probe cap state when it bound, the edge-case cap when it bound, and the count of `oversized` units, each with the same framing — a capped round is not an uncapped one. Consider stating explicitly that a unit flagged `oversized` yields a cell whose coverage claim is weaker, so `cr status` reports it as a qualified rather than a complete row.

finding: §2.3.3 requires every record in `claims.ndjson`, `units.ndjson`, `mapping.ndjson`, `findings.ndjson`, `probes.ndjson`, `runs.ndjson`, `intent-gaps.ndjson`, and `coverage.ndjson` to carry `head` and `round`, but five of the schemas that define those files list neither or only `head`: §3.3's claim table has `head` and no `round`; §3.4.6's unit fields have neither; §4.5.5's cell has `head` and no `round`; §5.2.4's run record has `head` and no `round`; §5.5's probe table has `head` and no `round`. §4.1.6 is a direct contradiction rather than an omission — it fixes `mapping.ndjson` at "one `{claim, unit}` pair per line". Because §6.1.3 rejects a record missing any required field and §6.1.4 rejects one carrying a computed field, I have to know for each agent-supplied file whether `round` is the agent's to write or `cr`'s to stamp, and the spec answers for neither.
suggestion: Add `round` (and `head` where missing) to the §3.3, §3.4.6, §4.5.5, §5.2.4 and §5.5 schemas, marking each `computed` where `cr` stamps it — the agent has no reliable way to know the round index. Reword §4.1.6 to say each line carries `{claim, unit}` plus the `head` and `round` `cr` stamps.

finding: `tests.probe_path_template`'s default is given as "`<root of the first `tests.globs` entry>/cr_probe_<probe-id><ext>`", and the row carefully defines `<root>` ("the longest leading path prefix free of `*`, `?`, and `[`") while `<ext>` is never defined anywhere in the document. Candidate sources are all plausible: the extension of the supplied `--test <file>` argument (§5.4.2), the suffix of the first `tests.globs` entry, a per-profile constant, or the empty string. The choice is not cosmetic — §5.4.2 places the gap probe's file at this path so "the runner's own discovery still finds the file", and §5.1.6's cleanliness check looks for "no file under the path `tests.probe_path_template` yields for any probe id". A wrong extension makes the runner skip the probe file (driving every gap probe to `no-tests-selected`) and makes the leftover-artefact check miss it. I cannot write the default-path test or the shipped-profile assertion in §2.4's own "each shipped profile MUST set it so the result matches its own `tests.globs`" without a definition.
suggestion: Define `<ext>` in the same row, e.g. the file extension of the path supplied to `--test`, including the leading dot, and empty when the supplied path has none. State the same for `<probe-id>` by pointing at §5.5's `p<n>` form, and give the resolved default for `laravel-pest` as a worked example.

finding: Nothing says which command runs rule detection and appends to `rule-stats.ndjson`. §2.6.1.6 mandates that "every hit, record, and dismissal MUST be appended", and §6.2.5 makes record-time `origin` stamping depend on those hit rows existing at the same head with the same path and line — so hits must be on disk before `cr record`. Two commands need them: §11 lists `cr rules check <pr>` ("Run mechanical rule detection over the diff") and §4.6.1 requires `cr review` to carry "the rule hits of §4.3.6" into every prompt. If both run detection, both append and the corpus grows a duplicate hit per invocation, which distorts §2.6.3.4's dead-rule window; if only one does, `cr review` must fail when `cr rules check` has not been run and no section says so. Separately, a "dismissal" is only knowable after the merged records arrive, so it can only be written by `cr record` — which the spec never states.
suggestion: Designate one owner: `cr rules check <pr>` performs detection and is the sole writer of hit rows, idempotent per `(rule id, path, line, head, round)` so a re-run does not double-append; `cr review` reads those rows and MUST fail with a hint when none exist for the current head; `cr record` writes the record and dismissal rows by comparing confirmed citations against the hits for that head.

finding: Rule detection and unit clustering scan different sets, and the spec never reconciles them. §2.6.1.1 evaluates a `detect` block over "the added and modified `RIGHT`-side lines of the diff" — the whole diff. §3.4.2 excludes files matching `ignore.globs` from clustering and §3.4.7 lists binary and generated files without clustering them, so those lines belong to no unit. §4.3.6 then requires a hit to be "attached to the unit that contains it" and §6.1 requires every record to carry a `unit`, so a hit in an unclustered file can never become a record and has no defined disposition. Meanwhile §2.6.1.6 requires every hit to be appended to `rule-stats.ndjson` regardless, which makes a rule that only ever fires on ignored or generated files look alive to §2.6.3.4's dead-rule report while producing nothing.
suggestion: Subordinate detection to clustering: state in §2.6.1.1 that a `detect` block is evaluated over the changed lines of the units of §3.4 only, so `ignore.globs`, binary, and generated files are out of reach by construction and every hit has a unit. If hits outside units are wanted for statistics, record them with an explicit `unattached: true` marker and exclude them from §2.6.3.4's liveness computation.

finding: §3.4 cannot decide whether a unit spans files. §3.4.4's clustering rules are all scoped "same file", and §3.4.5's split only ever narrows a cluster, so every unit has exactly one file. §3.4.6 nonetheless requires a unit to record "its **file paths**" plural and defines the unit hash over "the unit's changed lines taken file by file in ascending path order" — a pre-image that is only meaningful for a multi-file unit. Downstream rules inherit the confusion: §6.2.2 grades a probe by whether its `target` "falls inside that record's unit", and §3.4.6's own id ordering keys on "first file path then first changed line", both of which read as multi-file.
suggestion: Pick one. If units are single-file, change §3.4.6 to "its file path", drop the file-by-file clause from the hash pre-image, and simplify the id ordering to "file path then first changed line". If units may span files, §3.4.4 needs a rule that forms one, which today it does not have.

finding: `units.ndjson` is required by §2.3 and read by §4.6.1, §4.1, §4.3.6, §4.4.1 and §10.1.1, but its only writer is permissive: §3.7 says `cr brief` "MAY compute and persist the derived inputs of §3.3 through §3.6 — claims already recorded, units, threads, notes". The one place clustering is a MUST is §9.3.4, which fires only when the head has moved. So on a PR's first round nothing is obliged to produce units, and §4.6 does not say `cr review` computes them. I would have to invent one of two quite different designs: `cr review` clusters on demand, or it exits 4 with "run `cr brief` first".
suggestion: Make it a MUST in §3.7 — `cr brief` MUST compute and persist units, ingested threads, and the loaded notes for the round — and keep the MAY only for what is genuinely optional. Then add to §4.6 that `cr review` MUST exit 4 with a hint naming `cr brief <pr>` when no unit set exists for the current round and head, so there is exactly one producer.

finding: §4.1.7 makes `cr` derive `intent-gaps.ndjson` "mechanically as the claims of the current round mapped to zero units" on *each* successful `cr map record`, while §4.1.8 has `cr claims set-aside` stamp `set_aside_note` onto a gap entry. Nothing says the re-derivation preserves an existing stamp, so a second `cr map record` in the same round silently wipes every set-aside decision. §10.2.3 makes that observable: a round that was complete becomes incomplete again, with no event recorded and no way for the user to see why. As written I would implement re-derivation as a truncate-and-rewrite and introduce exactly this bug.
suggestion: Add to §4.1.7 that re-derivation MUST carry forward `set_aside_note` for any claim that is still mapped to zero units, and MUST drop it for a claim that has become mapped. State that a set-aside for a claim that no longer appears is discarded, and that neither carry-forward nor discard is silent — both belong in the round summary.

finding: §4.1.7 requires `intent-gaps.ndjson` to be derived "mechanically" from the current mapping on every successful `cr map record`, while §4.1.8 has `cr claims set-aside` stamp `set_aside_note` onto a gap entry. A mechanical re-derivation regenerates the entries from claims and mapping alone and has no way to carry the stamps forward, so any later `cr map record` — the expected case, since mapping is revised as review proceeds — silently discards every set-aside. §10.2.3 then re-blocks completeness on claims the reviewer already judged out of scope, with no report that a decision was reversed. The same erasure applies to `cr claims record`, which per §3.3.1 clears `mapping.ndjson` and thereby invalidates the derived gaps too.
suggestion: Make the set-aside decision durable independently of the derived file: store `set_aside_note` against the claim id (in `claims.ndjson` or a small side file) and have §4.1.7's derivation re-attach it to a regenerated entry for the same claim in the same round. State explicitly that re-derivation MUST preserve set-asides for claims that are still unmapped, and MUST report a set-aside that became moot because the claim is now mapped.

finding: §4.4.4 states that "a test-adequacy finding without a probe MUST be graded `argued`", but §6.2.1 says the grade "MUST be computed by `cr` from the record" with citations and the referenced probe as the only inputs, and §6.2 grades any record `cited` when it carries a resolvable citation with `origin: rule` or one outside its own unit. A test-adequacy finding that cites the existing test file it says lacks a case — the most natural citation for that axis — is therefore computed `cited`, not `argued`, and escapes §6.3's forcing to a question. §4.4.4's MUST is unimplementable as a separate rule, and the axis whose findings are most speculative is the one that quietly gains the assertion register.
suggestion: Decide which rule governs and delete the other. Either drop the grade mandate from §4.4.4 and let §6.2 rule (accepting that a cited test-adequacy finding may assert), or add an explicit exception to §6.2 stating that a record on the `test` axis with no `probe` is graded `argued` regardless of citations, with §4.4.4 cross-referencing it. The second preserves the trust economy; whichever is chosen must live in §6.2, since §6.2.1 makes that the only place a grade is decided.

finding: §4.5.1 defines a role as active partly by "§4.6.4 did not report it skipped", and §4.6.4 says "A role whose prerequisites are unmet MUST be reported as skipped with its reason" — but a role's prerequisites are enumerated nowhere. §4.5.2 and §4.5.3 give two *axis* prerequisites (no `tests.cmd`, no issue key), and §2.5's role schema has only `id`, `title`, `axis`, `instructions`, `focus`, and `profiles`, all of which §4.5.1 already handles separately. So §4.6.4 has no testable trigger: I cannot construct an input that makes a role skipped, which means I cannot test the branch at all. The gap has teeth because §4.5.6 makes `cr cells record` "reject with exit code 1 a cell naming ... an inactive role", and the skip verdict is a transient property of a `cr review` invocation with no specified persistence — `meta.json` lists "active roles" per §2.3 but no rule says which command writes it. One engineer recomputes activity at cells-record time (and accepts the cell); another reads a stored skip list (and rejects it).
suggestion: Either enumerate a role's prerequisites (or state that a role has none beyond its axis and `profiles`, in which case delete the §4.6.4 clause from §4.5.1's definition), and name the command that writes `meta.json`'s active-roles list and the point at which `cr cells record` reads it.

finding: §4.5.1 defines a role as active partly by "§4.6.4 did not report it skipped", but §4.6.4's report is produced by `cr review`, which per §4.6.1 emits prompts "for every active role" — the set it is being used to define. Beyond the circularity, the skip report is transient: §2.3's `meta.json` lists "active roles" but no section says when that field is written or whether it records §4.6.4's skips and reasons. Later commands cannot evaluate the predicate they are required to enforce — §4.5.6 must "reject with exit code 1 a cell naming ... an inactive role", and §10.2.2 requires "a complete row of cells for every active role" — so both depend on a fact no file is specified to hold.
suggestion: Break the cycle by naming role prerequisites directly in §4.5.1 (axis active, `profiles` matches, and any per-role prerequisite such as a symbol index for a reinvention role), and reduce §4.6.4 to reporting those same conditions rather than defining them. Then state in §4.6 that `cr review` writes the resolved active-role set with each skip reason to `meta.json` for the current round, so §4.5.6 and §10.2.2 have a durable basis.

finding: §4.5.5 requires every cell to carry "the head it was filled against" and "the unit hash of §3.4.6 it was filled for", and §10.2.2 makes completeness depend on that hash matching the unit's current hash. But cells arrive through `cr cells record` (§4.5.6), and nothing marks `head` or the unit hash as computed by `cr` the way §6.1 marks a record's computed fields and §3.3 marks `span_hash` and `issue_hash`. §6.1.4's rejection list governs records, not cells. An agent that supplies a stale or invented unit hash defeats §10.2.2's freshness check entirely, and cr has no basis to reject it — yet cr already knows the correct hash for the named unit id, so there is no reason for the agent to supply it.
suggestion: State in §4.5.6 that `cr` computes and stamps a cell's `head` and unit hash itself from the named unit id at the current head, and MUST reject with exit code 1 a cell arriving with either field, mirroring §3.3.1 and §6.1.4. The agent supplies only `unit`, `role`, the verdict, and the `na` reason.

finding: §6.2.1 and §6.2.2 prescribe opposite handling of the same record, and the conflict pushes the agent to discard disconfirming evidence. §6.2.1 says the grade "MUST be computed by cr from the record" with `citations` and the referenced probe record as the only inputs — so a record naming a probe that does not support it computes to `argued` and becomes a question, the safe outcome. §6.2.2 says "A record claiming `probed` without a valid same-head probe that supports it MUST be rejected with exit code 1." Which fires is undetermined, and §6.1.4 makes the trigger incoherent besides: it rejects outright any record arriving with a `grade` field, so a record cannot "claim `probed`" — leaving unclear whether §6.2.2 is about a `grade` value that cannot exist or about a `probe` reference that does. If the reject reading holds, a whole `cr record` run exits 1 because one probe came back non-supporting, and the agent's cheapest repair is to strip the `probe` reference and resubmit. That silently deletes the record of an experiment that was run and did not support the finding — the single most valuable thing in a trust economy, since §5.3.6 uses exactly that outcome to stop a finding being raised. The spec should never make deleting negative evidence the path of least resistance.
suggestion: Resolve in favour of downgrade. State that a record referencing a probe that does not support it MUST be graded `argued` (hence forced to a question by §6.3), that the `probe` reference MUST be retained on the record, and that the non-support and its reason MUST be reported in the round summary. Reserve exit code 1 for a `probe` id that names no probe record at all, and rewrite §6.2.2's trigger in terms of the `probe` field, since §6.1.4 already makes a submitted `grade` impossible.

finding: §8.1.3 says "A posted comment is exactly three regions in order: the §8.1.4 label, the agent body, and the §8.1.7 citation block", but both `cr`-owned regions are conditional: §8.1.4's label applies only to `kind=question` and §8.1.7's citation block only to a `cited` record. A `probed` finding therefore has one region, and a `cited` finding two — "exactly three" is false for the majority of records, and I cannot tell whether to emit empty delimited regions or omit them. The delimiter rule has the same problem: "The two `cr`-owned regions MUST be delimited by `<!-- cr:begin -->` and `<!-- cr:end -->`" describes one pair of markers for two regions that are not contiguous — the agent body sits between them — so the parser contract is undefined (one pair, two pairs, or named pairs).
suggestion: Rewrite §8.1.3 as "at most three regions, in this order" and state that a region absent by its own rule is omitted entirely rather than emitted empty. Give each `cr`-owned region its own delimiter pair and name them, e.g. `<!-- cr:begin label -->`…`<!-- cr:end label -->` and `<!-- cr:begin citations -->`…`<!-- cr:end citations -->`, so the discard-edits-inside rule has an unambiguous span to apply to.

finding: §9.3.1 makes every command that reads per-PR state compare heads and report both when they differ, but §9.3.2 only refuses "to draft, post, or probe". That leaves `cr review`, `cr map record`, `cr cells record`, `cr claims record`, and `cr record` free to run against a moved head — and each of them writes current-round state. Since §9.3.3 makes `cr brief` the only thing that advances the round, and nothing obliges the user to run it, the reachable state is: units and unit hashes from the old head, findings recorded carrying the new head, cells whose `unit_hash` per §4.5.5 no longer matches any unit, and §10.2.2's per-unit-hash check failing for a reason the user cannot act on. I cannot tell whether these commands should proceed, warn, or exit 4.
suggestion: Extend §9.3.2 to every command that writes per-PR state: at a differing head they MUST exit 4 naming both heads and hinting `cr brief <pr>`, leaving only the read-only reporters (`cr status`, `cr context`, `cr config`) and the explicitly exempt `cr post --reconcile` able to run. That also makes `cr brief` the single, unavoidable entry point into a round, which is what §9.3.3 already assumes.

finding: §9.3.2 bars only three verbs at a moved head — "refuse to draft, post, or probe" — while §9.3.3 makes `cr brief` the sole command that advances the round. Everything between the two is unguarded: `cr claims record`, `cr map record`, `cr cells record`, `cr record`, and `cr merge` all read and write per-PR state and are permitted to run after a force-push. Per §2.3.3 they stamp records with the new `head` but the old `round`, and those records name unit ids that §3.4.6 makes round-scoped and that were computed against the superseded diff. The state is internally inconsistent until `cr brief` runs and §9.3.4 marks it stale, and nothing tells the agent that the work it just recorded is void.
suggestion: Extend §9.3.2 to every command that writes per-PR state: at a differing head they MUST refuse with exit code 4, naming both heads and hinting `cr brief` as the next step. Keep the §9.3.2 exemption for `cr post --reconcile` and add one for read-only reporting such as `cr status` and `cr context`, which should report the divergence rather than fail.

finding: §10.2.2's second condition — "every one of those cells was filled for that unit's current unit hash per §3.4.6" — cannot fail in v0.1, so it buys no protection for the field and the comparison it costs. Within a round the head is pinned: §9.3.2 refuses to draft, post, or probe when the current head differs from the recorded head, and §9.3.3 makes a same-head `cr brief` idempotent, so units and their hashes are fixed for the round's life. When the head does move, §9.3.3 increments the round and §9.3.4 recomputes units, while §9.3.5 restricts every command to the current round's records — so a cell carrying a stale unit hash is never in scope to be compared. §4.5.5 therefore mandates a per-cell field whose only consumer is a check that is unreachable. This is the ceremony side of the lens: cost paid on every cell, with no reduction in the chance of a wrong assertion. It is not wrong to record the hash — §9.2.3 keeps the anchor content hash on the same forward-looking reasoning — but the spec should say that is why, rather than dressing it as an active completeness condition.
suggestion: Either drop the unit-hash clause from §10.2.2 and state in §4.5.5 that the unit hash is recorded for a v0.2 migration exactly as §9.2.3 records the anchor content hash, or name the scenario in v0.1 in which a cell's stored unit hash can differ from its unit's current one. If none exists, the honest form is the former.

finding: §9.3.6 requires a finding matching the posted index to be "dropped at merge and counted in the round summary", but §10.3's enumeration of the summary — raised, deduplicated, suppressed by thread, waived, forced to question, drafted, posted, discarded as `not-here`, discarded as `wrong`, plus the comment count, probe cap state, and payload hash — reads as the complete set and has no field for a posted-index drop. §10.1.6 likewise reports only "waivers applied and duplicates suppressed". The one drop that is invisible everywhere else has nowhere to be counted.
suggestion: Add "dropped as already posted" to §10.3's list and to §10.1.6's `cr status` line, and name it in §9.3.6 so the two sections agree on the field.

finding: The §11 command table still describes `cr brief <pr>` as "Read-only orientation payload for a PR", which §3.7 and §9.3.3 no longer support: `cr brief` opens a new round when the head has moved, incrementing the round index, storing the new head, moving records to `stale`, clearing `mapping.ndjson`, and recomputing units, threads, and claims. §3.7 was rewritten to say exactly this — "the one case where it changes state" — and the summary table was not.
suggestion: Change the §11 row to "Orientation payload; opens a new round when the head has moved (§3.7, §9.3.3)", so the command surface does not advertise a read-only guarantee the spec withdrew.

finding: §5.1.6's cleanliness check is defined as "no file under the path `tests.probe_path_template` yields for any probe id", which only works if the template actually varies with the probe id. §2.4 documents the default as containing `cr_probe_<probe-id><ext>` but never requires a configured template to contain the `<probe-id>` placeholder. A profile setting a fixed path passes validation, makes two probes in one round collide, and turns §5.1.6's "for any probe id" scan into a single-path check.
suggestion: Require in §2.4 that `tests.probe_path_template` contain the `<probe-id>` placeholder, aborting with exit code 3 naming the profile when it does not — the same treatment `tests.count_pattern` already gets for its capture-group count.

finding: §5.4.2's "An existing file at that path MUST abort with exit code 4" is unreachable as written. §5.1.6 runs "before every probe or test run" and defines a sandbox as unclean when any leftover probe artefact exists at a `tests.probe_path_template` path, and requires such a sandbox to be recreated. Recreation removes the file, so by the time §5.4.2 places its test the path is always free. The two requirements do not conflict in outcome, but one of them is dead code and I would not know which behaviour the user is meant to observe.
suggestion: Either drop the §5.4.2 abort and point at §5.1.6's recreation, or scope it to the case §5.1.6 cannot cover — a tracked file already committed at the template path, which recreation restores rather than removes — and say that is what the exit 4 means.

finding: §6.4.1 deduplicates by `(anchor.path, anchor.line, class)` and §7.4.1 keys a waiver by `(anchor.path, class, normalised hash of the anchored lines)`; neither includes `anchor.side`, although §9.2 makes `side` part of every anchor and §6.1.2 resolves the two sides against different trees (head for `RIGHT`, merge base for `LEFT`). Two records of the same class at the same numeric line in the same file — one about an added line, one about a deleted line — therefore collapse into one duplicate group, and a waiver written for one silences the other. The same omission propagates to §9.3.6's posted index, which is "keyed exactly as a §7.4.1 waiver", so a posted `RIGHT` finding drops a distinct `LEFT` finding at merge before it is ever written to `findings.ndjson`.
suggestion: Add `anchor.side` to the §6.4.1 dedup key and to the §7.4.1 waiver key, and note in §9.3.6 that the posted index inherits it.
